function.name: telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get
function.description: Retrieves specified telemetry information for a network interface within a given fabric, node, and pod, filtered by the interface and information types. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

fabricName.description: The name of the fabric to limit the nodes pertaining to the given fabric name.

nodeId.description: The identifier of the node to limit the results pertaining to the given node ID.

podId.description: The identifier of the pod to limit the results pertaining to the given pod ID.

interfaceType.description: The type of the interface to limit the results pertaining to the given interface type.

infoType.description: The type of information to retrieve about the interface.

message.content:
Below is a quick‑start guide showing **how** you would pull “all nodes” belonging to the *test‑de* fabric from a device whose management IP is 23.31.32.1.  
(The exact URL paths depend on your platform – the examples below follow the common Cisco ACI/APIC style REST API.)

---

### 1️⃣  Get the full list of nodes in the fabric  

```bash
curl -k \
     -u admin:<password> \                     # replace <password>
     https://23.31.32.1/api/node/class/fabricNode.json
```

| Field | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| `dn`  | Distinguished Name – contains the fabric name (`topology`) |
| `name`| Node hostname/IP |
| `id`  | Numerical node id |

#### Filter for *test‑de*

If you prefer filtering server‑side instead of pulling everything into your script, add a query‑filter:

```bash
https://23.31.32.1/api/node/class/fabricNode.json?
    query-target-filter="eq(fabricNode.name,'test-de')"
```

*(Note: Some APIs don’t support direct equality filters on the top‑level class; you may need to post‑process locally.)*

---

### 2️⃣  Pull detailed per‑node telemetry (optional)

Once you’ve identified the node IDs, you can drill down further—for instance, to see interface statistics or errors—using the helper function you mentioned:

```python
from functions import telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get

result = telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get({
    "fabricName": "test-de",          # our target fabric
    "nodeId":   101,                  # <-- pick from step 1 output
    "podId":    0,                    # usually 0 unless multi‑pod
    "interfaceType":"ethernet",       # choose based on interest
    "infoType":"statistics"           # could also be "status","errors"
})
print(result)
```

> ⚠️ **Important:** This helper works at the *interface level*. If you just want a high‑level view of the node itself (CPU load, memory usage, health), look for a dedicated “node” telemetry endpoint such as:
> 
> ```
> https://23.31.32.1/api/node/class/sysHealthInst.json
> ```

---

### 3️⃣  Quick sanity check – ping the fabric controller

Before hitting the API, make sure you can reach the controller:

```bash
ping -c 3 23.31.32.1
```

A successful reply confirms connectivity; otherwise double‑check firewall rules or VPN settings.

---

## TL;DR Summary

| Step | What to do | Why |
|------|------------|-----|
| 1 | Call `/api/node/class/fabricNode.json` | Enumerate all nodes in the fabric |
| 2 | Optionally filter by `"name=='test-de'"` | Narrow to the desired fabric |
| 3 | Extract `id`, `name`, etc. | These values feed subsequent calls |
| 4 | Use those IDs with `telemetry_flowrules_interfaceInfo_get()` | Retrieve per‑interface stats/status/errors |

Feel free to paste the JSON payload here if you hit any snags parsing the result!
